doc.title: Rob Mounsey interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 9, 2025

title: Gold records and the 'You Can Call Me Al' horn arrangement for Paul Simon
summary: He explains the Graceland and Gaucho gold records and how he wrote the two-bar horn line for Paul Simon and Roy Halee, with Ronnie Cuber on bass saxophone, and went uncredited.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: To wrap up can you — we got a glimpse of a couple of gold records on your wall. You want to tell us about that?

Oh they just happened to be over the piano. One is a triple platinum for Paul Simon “Graceland,” and the other one is for Steely Dan “Gaucho.” There’s some more over there back there — “Graceland” harbors my —maybe my most heard horn arrangement of all time, which is the two-bar horn arrangement on “You Can Call Me Al” [scats] which millions and millions and millions of people have heard.
Oh my.
Yeah. It probably took five minutes to write it, and they left the credit off the album. Yeah.
Oh.
Yeah so I was kind of, like a little bugged about that.
How did that happen? You were listening to the track and it just like, you’re humming to yourself? I mean can you describe that?

Paul and Roy Halee asked me. I was in the studio with them and they asked me, “Can you make a brass section play this figure that the rhythm guitar is playing.” It was of the African rhythm guitarists. I’m sorry I don’t remember his name.
Ray Phiri?

Ray Phiri, maybe. Or there’s another guy’s name starts with a V. And it was just a rhythm guitar part. They said, “Can you make a brass section play that and by the way we really want to have a bass saxophone on the bottom, a B flat bass saxophone. I said sure.
Howard Johnson.
No I don’t think so. I think it was Ronnie Cuber actually.
Oh. But the bass saxophone didn’t come in ‘til later. Is that correct?
No I think it’s in the whole way, unless they took it out of the mix.
Well all right.
And it’s two bars over and over except for the one time it’s different.
[scats]

Yeah. [scats] that one time. So we’re madly counting, “36, 37, here it comes.” And you know it was very quick and very easy but I was so excited. I finally did an arrangement for a Paul Simon record. I was a huge Paul Simon fan, and they left the credit off the album. But it’s okay. People know now that I did it for them.
I’m going to tell all my friends too.
Well Roy Halee made a big point of announcing that so —
I love the fact that it starts with a rest.

Yeah. Right. One [scats]. Yes it’s rests on the downbeats of both bars. Yeah. But it’s just what the rhythm guitarist played. Like give it to three trumpets and three trombones and a bass saxophone and make the registers work nice. I think actually toward the end somewhere it jumps up one inversion.
